extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and educated general readers interested in sexual selection and comparative anatomy
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate morphological, behavioral, ontogenetic, and comparative indicators that a trait has been shaped by sexual selection (including male–male competition and female choice), with attention to alternative explanations such as natural selection, direct environmental effects, and inheritance patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental timing as evidence (traits appear near maturity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When conspicuous colours or ornaments are not developed until near maturity, this timing is evidence that they have been acquired through sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin: "When the colours are diversified and strongly pronounced, when they are not developed until near maturity... we can hardly avoid the conclusion that they have been acquired through sexual selection for the sake of ornament." Examples: many mammal and monkey colourings and facial ornamentation which only appear or intensify at sexual maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex-limited expression and castration loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits that are chiefly or exclusively expressed in one sex and that disappear after emasculation (castration) indicate origin by sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that many secondary sexual characters are transmitted exclusively to the same sex and are lost after emasculation. Use as diagnostic: if emasculation abolishes the trait, sexual selection is a strong explanatory hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater ornamentation/contrast in males
rubrics_metrics.description: When males exhibit darker, more strongly-contrasted, or otherwise more elaborate coloration/ornamentation than females, sexual selection acting primarily on males is a likely cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed across mammals and Quadrumana: males commonly show stronger colours or ornamentation. Example: antelopes and some Felis species where males are brighter; also beard/crest development in male monkeys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with other secondary sexual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Conspicuous colours or ornaments that occur together with other secondary sexual characters (weapons, size differences, crests, behavioural displays) within the same groups point to sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin: "That conspicuous and diversified colours... are as a general rule associated in the same groups and sub-groups with other secondary sexual characters serving for war or for ornament." Use co-occurrence across characters as corroborative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornaments present in both sexes but likely sexually selected
rubrics_metrics.description: When both sexes bear conspicuous, curiously arranged coloration or ornamentation that has no apparent protective function, analogy with male-limited ornamentation suggests sexual selection as the origin, possibly transmitted equally to both sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that conspicuous colours in both sexes, especially when apparently useless for protection and associated with other ornaments, are best explained by sexual selection even if transmitted to both sexes. Examples: many monkeys with both sexes coloured similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of battle / male–male competition indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Features such as greater size, strength, pugnacity, specialized weapons (horns, enlarged canines), or behavioural tendencies for fighting in males indicate modification by sexual selection via competition between males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's 'law of battle'—male traits that aid in defeating rivals (size, horns, tusks, courage) are often selected through contests for females. Distinguish from traits favored by general struggle for life by their sex-limited use and correlation with mating contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontogenetic retention as phylogenetic signal (juvenile markings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of juvenile markings (spots, stripes) across many species' young but not adults suggests inheritance from an ancient, spotted/striped progenitor; juvenile traits can reveal ancestral states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin describes gradations from always-spotted species to species without spots, and uses fawn spots in deer, pig and tapir young to infer ancestral striped/spotted condition. Use developmental series and comparative ontogeny to infer ancestral characters and their loss in adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative explanations must be considered (natural selection, direct effects, unknown causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all conspicuous or sex-differentiated traits are due to sexual selection; they may arise via natural selection (crypsis), direct action of conditions of life, simple variation, or unknown factors—these alternatives must be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin discusses, for example, loss of stripes/spots in adults possibly due to natural selection for concealment, and domestic animal variation (donkeys losing stripes). Evaluate ecological utility, life-history, and domestication/comparative evidence before attributing traits solely to sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative geography and phyletic patterns as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic/clade-specific patterns (e.g., African vs. Asiatic asinine stripes) and correlated presence/absence across related species can indicate selective pressures or inheritance affecting ornamentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites distributional differences (Asinus species striped in Africa but not Asia) as evidence that must be reconciled with selection or inheritance hypotheses. Use comparative distribution and phylogenetic patterns to test hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentation unlikely from mere variability (improbability argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the arrangement or colour of hair/feathers/skin is oddly arranged or highly elaborate, it is scarcely conceivable to be due to mere variability without selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses this improbability as an argument for sexual selection (e.g., curious crests and tufts of monkeys). Treat extreme, structured, or repeated patterns as more plausibly produced/maintained by selection than by random variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence from domesticated forms and reversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes or reappearance of primitive traits in domesticated or aberrant individuals (reversion) can indicate ancestral conditions and inform selection hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: occasional projecting canine teeth in humans as reversion to ancestor state; loss of stripes in domestic asses. Use domestication and atavism evidence cautiously to infer ancestral states and selective histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Olfactory and vocal traits as possible sexual signals (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful odours produced by males during breeding and modifications of voice may serve to attract mates and thus be products of sexual selection, though certainty varies by trait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin: odour glands acquired through sexual selection are plausible; voice is more doubtful because vocal organs may be strengthened by use in maturity and transmitted to the same sex. Evaluate behavioural context, seasonality, sex-specificity, and experimental/observational evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism variability across races/species as evidence of selection intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: High variability of secondary sexual characters among males (greater male–male variance) and large differences between sexes in some races/species indicate stronger or more recent sexual selection acting on males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes male characters vary more between races and tribes (e.g., beard development across human populations), suggesting that males have been chiefly modified during divergence. Use measures of variance and cross-population comparisons to infer selection regimes.
